To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

mutational meltdown is a process by which the accumulation of deletrious mutations causes the extinction of small populations, that it is more severe when selection is weak and mutation is strong, that it does not require a large number of loci, that it can be avoided by recombination, that it can occur in asexual populations as well as sexual ones, and that the effective mutation load can be reduced by increasing the variance of the mutational effects.

mutational load is a function of population size and the strength of selection and that the accumulation of mutations in small sexual populations leads to a progressive loss of genetic variation that ultimately causes extinction.

(i) small populations of asexually reproducing organisms have characteristic extinction times; (ii) this time is insensitive to carrying capacity; (iii) it can be predicted from the mutation rate and the distribution of mutational effects; (iv) it is much longer than the time required to accumulate a large mutation load; and (v) the extinction time can be substantially reduced by recombination.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of finite, nonrecombining, populations in which the rate of accumulation of new mutations is constant and selection is weak relative to mutation.
a class of extinction models that can be used to predict the fate of a population in the presence of deleterious mutation, selection and random genetic drift.
the joint effects of mutation and random genetic drift in small populations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the accumulation of deleteri­ous mutations is the major cause of the extinction of small populations.
, in the absence of selection, the probability of fixation of a mutation is proportional to its selective disadvantage.
the accumulation of mutations is a major cause of population extinction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
selection is a much more potent force in finite populations than is usually recognized.
the mutational meltdown model provides a simple and general framework for the evolution of mutation‐induced extinction.
the mutation load, as defined in the classical population genetics literature, is an inadequate measure of the mutational burden on a finite population.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mutation load can be an important factor in the extinction of small populations.
the survival of small populations is strongly influenced by the mutation load and that the effective mutation load can be substantially reduced by recombination.
the mutation load can be a significant determinant of population survival.
